newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK, Taiwan, China stocks rise despite Deng worries.
newsitem.headline: HK, Taiwan, China stocks rise despite Deng worries.

text.p: Stock markets in Hong Kong, Taiwan and China closed higher on Wednesday as concern over the health of China's paramount leader Deng Xiaoping began to dissipate.

Hong Kong stocks weakened slightly after opening higher, and then bounced back, leaving the Hang Seng Index little changed. It ended up 3.38 points, or 0.03 percent, at 13,106.32. It shed 41.68 points, or 0.32 percent on Tuesday.

"His health has been under question for a while and as such the market has had to think about this a number of times to the point where you would have expected the market to discount the fact that he won't be around forever," said Julian Ings Chambers, assistant director at BZW Securities.
After falling sharply on Monday and Tuesday, stocks in China's two markets, Shanghai and Shenzhen, moved higher on Wednesday.
Traders said remarks from Beijing's foreign ministry that there had been no major change in Deng's health prompted a modest recovery.
"The foreign ministry statement helped improve sentiment a little, pushing the index up in a technical rebound this morning," one broker said.
"But concerns over Deng's health have not disappeared and room for further rises will be limited," he added.
Shenzhen's domestic A share index jumped 20.49 points, or 6.07 percent to close at 358.13 points, while the foreign-owned B share index gained 4.03 points, or 2.93 percent, to 141.75 points.
The A share index had lost 9.76 percent on Tuesday, while the B shares shed 9.58 percent.
Shanghai's A share index was up 72.17 points, or 7.74 percent to 1004.95 points after losing 8.97 percent on Tuesday.

Hong Kong's flat performance reflected a preference among investors to shift their funds out of the territory as a result of the uncertainty over Deng's health. "People are hesitant to get in now," one analyst said.
Fears that the health of Deng, 92, had worsened, were sparked after the country's leaders cut short out-of-town trips.
Japan's Kyodo news agency said Deng suffered a brain haemorrhage last Friday and had been taken to hospital.
Hong Kong's Ming Pao newspaper said Deng was recuperating at home with a team of doctors attending to him.
Taiwan shares closed higher, but off early highs, as worries receded that the central bank would take measures to curb the market's recent wild gains.
Concern over Deng's health, which had hit the market on Tuesday, were not a factor on Wednesday.
The weighted index ended 14.82 points, or 0.19 percent higher, at 7,656.85.
Elsewhere in Asia, Tokyo stocks ended slightly higher after a directionless session aided by expectations of strong earnings for chemical and steel shares.
The key Nikkei 225 average gained 128.37 points, or 0.69 percent, to 18,599.12.
Trading was quiet in other Asian markets, with South Korean stocks ending up 1.54 points, or 0.22 percent, at 708.48, and Thai shares 6.44 points, or 0.92 percent higher, at 706.59.
The U.S. dollar was steady against the Japanese yen and German mark.
Early gains were eroded after Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer said the dollar's rise was the result of an overdue correction and that he hoped the correction had ended.
The dollar was quoted at 123.94/99 yen, compared with 123.82/90 in New York overnight, and at 1.6860/65 marks, compared with 1.6850/60.
